summary:
Antioquia department stands under Colombia's national legal framework, among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry trans and non-binary markers from November 2025. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office.

Access to premises is protected by court order. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.

Antioquia is also a site of lethal violence. On 5 April 2025 a 28-second video went viral showing 32-year-old Sara Millerey González Borja beaten and thrown into a waterway in Bello, in broad daylight while onlookers filmed; she could not swim and drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was." President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and protests were held in several cities. She was the third LGBTQ person killed in Bello in 2025; the first two victims were gay men.

Treatment and official conduct compounded the case. A clinic reportedly did not treat Millerey as an emergency "because she didn't get shot", and she died of cardiac arrest the following afternoon. Medellín's city hall was criticised for using her pre-transition name.

Killings continue at scale. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 alone, and the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025. More than 40 transgender women were killed in 2023, with eight more between February and April 2024, national figures that also cover Antioquia.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee noted concern. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.
tangentialFactors:
Some of the targeting is organised and rooted in the country's decades-long civil conflict. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024, stating that "all will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". In Caquetá, where ex-rebel structures persist despite the 2016 peace agreement, flyer campaigns distributed on streets and WhatsApp announce a "social cleansing" of "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots"; trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to move twice after death threats from armed men, and trans women in the department have few options beyond sex work.

Killings of queer Colombians continued after the Millerey case, described in reporting as calculated brutality. The national 2023 and early-2024 tallies cited for Antioquia are drawn from reporting on Caquetá, and no Antioquia-specific source covers those figures or the southern-department flyer campaigns.
localsOnly:
The marker-change procedure is administrative: trans Colombians sign a document before a notary, with no judicial order, bodily inspection or psychiatric assessment. The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Residents in Antioquia can rely on the same constitutional judgments on premises access and detainee treatment as elsewhere in Colombia, and on the July 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment of 15 former rebels, which recognised conflict-driven violence against LGBTI people as gender persecution and a crime against humanity.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in this inventory attributes the national 2023 and early-2024 trans homicide tallies, or the armed-group flyer campaigns in Guajira and Caquetá, to incidents inside Antioquia; they are reported as national or other-department figures that include Antioquia within the national count.

Unresolved: the inventory contains no Antioquia-specific reporting on enforcement of the national rulings on premises access, on access to gender-affirming care in the department, or on detention conditions for trans people in Antioquia's own prisons. The status of pending national legislation on trans rights is not sourced here.
